crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Expense Fraud
children.blurb: Expense fraud covers false, inflated, or duplicate expense claims, personal costs submitted as business expenses, and collusion between employees, approvers, or vendors.

children.name: Money Laundering Networks
children.blurb: This page covers the use of artificial intelligence to identify, map, and disrupt money laundering networks.

children.name: Phantom Vendors and Procurement Fraud
children.blurb: Phantom vendors are supplier records that exist only on paper or in a system, created to route payments to a fraudster rather than a real provider of goods or services.

children.name: Communication Forensics
children.blurb: Communication forensics applies analytical methods to emails, chat logs, call recordings, and other message data to uncover fraud, reconstruct events, and support investigations.

children.name: Tracing and Recovering Digital Assets
children.blurb: Tracing and recovering digital assets covers the identification, location, and legal recovery of funds or tokenized property that have been moved through cryptocurrency wallets, exchanges, decentralized finance protocols, and other digital channels.

sections.body: Fraud detection and forensics applies machine learning to financial records, communications, and transaction trails to find patterns that indicate deception or criminal activity. In expense fraud, systems compare receipts, timestamps, and employee spending against historical norms to flag duplicate or inflated claims. For money laundering, graph algorithms group accounts and transactions to expose layering and structuring across many banks. Vendor fraud tools match supplier names, addresses, and bank details to spot shell companies and duplicate invoices. Communication forensics uses language models to review emails and chat logs for signs of collusion or concealment. Digital asset tracing follows cryptocurrency flows across public ledgers to identify wallets and exchanges linked to fraud.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The most reliable work happens where fraud patterns are stable and data is structured, such as duplicate invoice detection and known money laundering typologies. These systems still produce many false positives, so human review remains standard. Novel or adaptive fraud is harder, because models trained on past cases miss new schemes. Explainability is a real limit, as regulators and courts often need a clear reason for a flag that a neural network cannot easily provide. Cross border asset recovery is also constrained by inconsistent legal cooperation and privacy rules.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: Expense Fraud explains how machine learning reviews employee spending for anomalies like split purchases or out of policy reimbursements. Money Laundering Networks covers graph based detection of accounts that move funds in circular or layered patterns. Phantom Vendors and Procurement Fraud focuses on supplier identity resolution and invoice matching to catch fake or duplicate vendors. Communication Forensics describes how language models and metadata analysis surface coordination or concealment in emails and messages. Tracing and Recovering Digital Assets walks through blockchain analytics, wallet clustering, and the practical steps for freezing or returning stolen funds. Together these pages move from internal employee fraud to external network fraud, then to the evidence and asset recovery stages.
